title: ECMO & Advanced Circulatory Support
sources: Critical Vector — ECMO & Advanced Circulatory Support (VA-ECMO physiology, cannulation, indications, evidence)
Lorusso R et al. ELSO Interim Guidelines for VA-ECMO in Adult Cardiac Patients. ASAIO J 2021;67:827-844
Schmidt M et al. SAVE score. Eur Heart J 2015;36:2246-2256

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV ECMO guide: circuit, cannulation strategies, indications/contraindications, SAVE risk classes, the ECMO-CS/ECLS-SHOCK 'now vs if-and-when' question, weaning readiness and failure predictors.

summary: VA-ECMO replaces both the heart and the lung (drains venous blood, oxygenates it, returns it under arterial pressure). VV-ECMO supports gas exchange only — the native heart still does the circulating. Overall adult VA-ECMO survival to discharge is ~41% but varies enormously by indication.

items: VA-ECMO: circulatory + gas-exchange support. Drainage cannula (femoral vein → IVC, or central RA) → centrifugal pump → membrane oxygenator → return cannula (femoral artery, axillary, or central aorta). A distal perfusion line off a femoral arterial cannula prevents limb ischemia.
VV-ECMO: gas exchange only (severe ARDS refractory to lung-protective ventilation ± prone ± neuromuscular blockade — EOLIA population). The native heart must be adequate.

rows: Fastest emergency approach — percutaneous, no sternotomy. Risk: differential hypoxia (Harlequin / North–South syndrome) — a still-ejecting LV pumps deoxygenated blood from poorly-functioning native lungs to the head and coronaries while the retrograde ECMO flow oxygenates the lower body. Monitor the RIGHT radial ABG / SpO2.
Femoral VA plus an Impella, IABP, or surgical vent to offload a distending LV — addresses the afterload the retrograde flow imposes on a failing ventricle (pulmonary edema, LV thrombus risk).
Direct aortic + RA cannulation, usually post-cardiotomy — better flow, more invasive, needs chest access.
Three-cannula configuration — a second return or drainage site to manage combined cardiac + respiratory failure or correct differential hypoxia.

items: Medical: AMI cardiogenic shock, fulminant myocarditis, cardiotoxic drug intoxication, end-stage dilated/ischemic cardiomyopathy, massive PE, refractory arrhythmia.
Surgical: failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass, post-cardiotomy shock, post-transplant primary graft failure.
Absolute contraindication: an irreversible, non-recoverable condition without transplant or durable-VAD candidacy; unwitnessed arrest with prolonged downtime and poor neuro prognosis.
Relative: advanced age (an independent mortality predictor, not a hard cutoff), significant comorbidity burden, cognitive impairment, inadequate social support.

body.text: 12 pre-cannulation variables (age, weight, diagnosis, chronic renal failure, pre-ECMO organ failures, peak inspiratory pressure, intubation duration, pre-ECMO cardiac arrest, pulse pressure, diastolic pressure, bicarbonate). Use it to inform the candidacy / goals-of-care conversation before the decision is final.

ECMO-CS (Circulation 2023): immediate VA-ECMO did NOT improve outcomes over an early-conservative strategy in severe / rapidly deteriorating cardiogenic shock — but 39% of the conservative arm crossed over to ECMO or other MCS on deterioration. ECLS-SHOCK (NEJM 2023): routine early ECLS in infarct-related cardiogenic shock did not reduce 30-day mortality and increased bleeding and vascular complications. The question is not 'ECMO or not' but 'ECMO now, or ECMO if and when deterioration demands it' — reserve immediate cannulation for the patient who is actively failing maximal support.

items: Weaning readiness: gas exchange maintained at FiO2 < 30%, low sweep-gas flow, stable hemodynamics on minimal pump flow.
Weaning trial: gradual flow reduction with continuous echo + hemodynamic monitoring; a controlled backflow trial assesses true native cardiac recovery.
Failure predictors: pre-existing ischemic heart disease, pre-weaning LVEF ≤ 25%, post-test SBP ≤ 120, ECMO duration > 7 days.
Common complications: bleeding, stroke, cannulation-site vascular injury, limb ischemia (peripheral arterial), infection, hemolysis.
